place.en: The Si · Outside the stone door

setup.zh: 三天后，潮水要回来了。你不早不晚，混在人群里出来，空着手，一身泥。「捡到什么了？」「一撮土。」
setup.en: Three days later the tide is coming back. You come out neither early nor late, in the crowd, empty-handed and muddy. "Find anything?" "A pinch of earth."

recap.zh: 秘境关门前一个时辰，困阵松了，你在崖下还了马小宝二十三下。秘境关了。名牌进去四百一十七块，收回一百八十三块；马小宝他们出来五个，少了孟有田——周衡在账簿上画了一道红杠，写名字写到天黑。你在本子上记下「冬月初一。左崖。邹青松。」，记在自己名下；「冬月初二夜。左崖。孟有田。」，没有写在谁的名下。离腊月初八的宗门大比，冬月初一周衡当面说过：内门外门一起比，冠军，筑基丹一枚，全观一年就这一颗。
recap.en: An hour before the realm shut, the binding let go, and at the foot of the cliff you paid Ma Xiaobao back his twenty-three. The hidden realm closed. Four hundred and seventeen name tablets went in, a hundred and eighty-three came back; of Ma Xiaobao's lot five came out, Meng Youtian missing — Zhou Heng drew a red line in his ledger and wrote names until dark. In your notebook: "First of the eleventh month. The left cliff. Zou Qingsong." — under your own name; "Second night of the eleventh month. The left cliff. Meng Youtian." — under no one's. The sect contest is on the eighth of the twelfth; Zhou Heng said it to your face on the first of the eleventh: inner court and outer court together, the champion gets one Foundation pill — one a year, for the whole temple.

zh: 三天后，秘境关闭。你空着手出来。
冬月初二夜。左崖。孟有田。——没写在谁的名下。
en: Three days on, the hidden realm closes. You come out empty-handed.
Second night of the eleventh month. The left cliff. Meng Youtian. — under no one's name.

story.zh:
话分两头。那一日小满往左，阿禾往右——右边人多，刀先落在别人头上——可落下来的刀，也是右边多。

她照着肚子里那张地图走。第二间石室门口，地上第三块石板踩上去会翻——她站在旁边，喊了一声「别踩第三块」。一个听了；一个没来得及听，给后头一个锦袍公子一肘子拐开，掉了下去，坑里「哎哟」一声，是孙二狗的嗓子。她给人群推着往前走，回头喊了第二声，没有人应。

石桥窄，只容一个人。她走到桥头，桥当中黑地里撞上了两个人，一个本观的灰袍，一个青萍的青袍，隔着三步站住了，谁也看不清谁的脸。站了很久，两个人都不动，都不让。灰袍伸手往怀里一摸——青袍的剑先出了鞘。灰袍倒下去，手里攥着的，是一只火折子。青袍跨过他，过了桥。阿禾在桥头的石头后头蹲了一炷香，才敢过去。

桥那头的灵草园子，最后一株给人连根拔了。两个本观的老弟子把一个锦袍公子按进泥里，按到他不动了，才松手，蹲在泥里分那株草，一人一半；又翻他的荷包，灵石五块，一人两块，多出来那一块，两个人猜拳。园子底下那道干河床，地图上画的是水；今年水退得低，露了底，石缝里一丛一丛全是灵草，上中下三品都有，壁上一道铜矿。人都往下涌。往下只有一道石坎，一人宽。坎口站着内门的祁长松，八层，两只脚钉在那里；人涌到他跟前，推他，挤他，像水撞上一根桩，撞不动，只好从两边分开，又流回来。坎底下，那四个九层一丛一丛地拔，拔一丛，往袖里一揣，看都不看是几品。拔够了上来，祁长松才挪开一步。

阿禾没有去抢。她绕到河床边上，那里有一片地，是黑的，黑得发亮，一根草也不长，跟石坳村她家那面坡田，一个样子。黑地的边上，偏偏冒着一株草，三片叶子，紫里透金：「紫须芝，一株抵三块灵石。」三块灵石，是外门一个月的份例。她蹲下去，指头底下的黑土一松，露出半粒东西来，黑的，硬得像石子：是谷，烧焦了一样的谷。她拿指甲再往下抠——那片黑地底下，一垄一垄，排得整整齐齐。很久很久以前，这里有人种过地。那株紫须芝的根，正缠在那一垄谷里：拔草，便连根带谷翻成一团烂泥；抠谷，草便保不住。她低下头，一粒一粒，抠出三粒来。

抠出第三粒，她脖子后头一烫。一条一尺来长的火蛇搭在她肩膀上，蛇头贴着她的脖子，烫得汗毛一根一根卷了起来。身后那人笑眯眯的，白净脸，赭黄袍子：「小丫头，蹲着找什么呢？捡土么？」他弯腰把那株紫须芝连根拔了，揣进怀里，「这园子拔秃了。你那张地图，给我。」阿禾道：「没有图。我背下来了。」那人道：「那就背。背错一个字——」火蛇往里一收，她脖子上那一圈皮肉「滋」的一声。阿禾便背：长廊几步一拐，哪一块石板会翻，三间石室，石桥，园子，一口气背下来，声音一个字也没抖，背到末了：「左崖。十年前下去三个，上来一个……没人去。」那人「哦」了一声：「没人去的地方，才有东西。」火蛇从她脖子上滑下来，钻回了葫芦。他往回走了，走得很快。

阿禾蹲在黑地边上，半天没站起来。脖子上一圈燎泡，她抓了一把凉土按着。她把三粒黑谷包进一小块布里，跟袄襟里缝着的那三十粒禾种挨在一处，掏出小本子记了一笔：**冬月初一。秘境。紫须芝一株，让了。谷，三粒，黑的，不能吃。**想了想，又添了一行：**有人种过。**

第三天天亮以后，崖上没有声音了。小满坐在石台前，手还在抖。他把本子摊在膝盖上，翻到后一页——抄的是褚先生下堂前摇头晃脑念的五句，念完了，戒尺往桌上一敲：「《尚书》{典=shangshu-hongfan}上的，背！」他小声念了一遍：「水曰润下，火曰炎上，木曰曲直，金曰从革，土爰稼穑。」木牌里那个声音懒懒地道：「五样脾气。土是能种东西的——种不出东西的，不叫土。你推着它们走一圈。」

他便推。一股凉从丹田里起，拐个弯一热，热沉成暖，暖硬进骨头，又凉下来渗回丹田——木、火、土、金、水，转了一圈。他想起了他家的灶：柴烧成火，火烧成灰，灰拿去肥地，地里长出秆子，秆子晒干了，又塞回灶膛。褚先生摇头晃脑讲了半天的，他娘一辈子天天在做。他的手，不抖了。

那天晌午，小满把空玉匣合上，放回石台正中，摆得端端正正；又在那四个空坑旁边蹲下，拿手掌量了一遍：七拃，没错。坑沿上的鼎苔，他抠了一小撮，包进帕子里。他对着四个空坑，拱了拱手，说不上为什么，银月也没有问他拱的是谁。

他走出那道墙。墙敞着，那口铁锅还趴在窝里，脖子上插着剑。崖壁上那一圈青白的光还亮着，五个人还贴在上头，饿得连哼都哼不出来了。最外沿，紧挨着那道黑口子的地方，还贴着一件灰袍子，两只袖子张开，领口撕开了，空的，里头没有人，给那一圈光粘在石头上，像一个人刚刚从里头走了出去。石台外沿那根锈烂的铁橛子跟前，崖沿上有几道新刮出来的白印子，是指甲刮的，一道比一道短。

小满在那几道白印子跟前站了一会儿。他没有往黑里望。

他没有走。他在铁橛子跟前坐下，背对着崖壁，把那把缺了牙的短刀横在膝盖上，等。猎户蹲一头鹿，一蹲一天，是常事。

石门合上前一个时辰，崖壁上那一圈青白的光，灭了。五个人扑通扑通掉在石台上，趴了半天，才一个一个爬起来。黑地里，马小宝看清了铁橛子跟前坐着的那一个，眼睛慢慢亮了：「……一个二层。」他嗓子饿得发哑，笑还是那个笑，「三天没吃饭，收拾你，也够了。」他扑了上来。

小满站起身，一拳迎在他鼻梁上。

「一。」

马小宝往后一仰，还没仰下去，第二拳到了。「二。」小满一下一下地数，不快，不慢，像他爹剥兔子皮，有个次第：鼻梁，左肋，右肋，肚子。四层的灵力，他只使了三成——使足了，这人就没了。四个跟班贴着崖根站成一排，没有一个敢动，他也一个没碰。数到「二十三」，最后一下不轻不重，点在马小宝的肩膀上，倒像是给这件事盖了个戳。

马小宝蜷在地上，抱着脑袋，两只眼睛肿成了两条缝。小满蹲下来：「十月十二，柴房，二十三下。还你了。一下不多，一下不少。」他站起身要走，地上落下一句话来，声音压得极低：「沈小满。」

小满站住了。马小宝脸贴着石头，一个字一个字地道：「墙里头，你听见什么了？」小满道：「听见了。」马小宝没有作声，过了好一会儿，才又道：「进秘境前，我爹的信到了。腊月里，他亲自坐船来，给我捎丹，还捎一面镜子——正月初五夜里，就在你家院子里，白衣仙长亲手交给我爹的那一面；火把，是我举的。仙长说了，照着了，有赏。」他喘了一口气，「大比台上，我当着全观，拿它照一照你。你这三天在墙后头干了什么，照得出来。你听见了什么——到了台上，你一个字也说不出来。」

小满没有答话。胸口的木牌，在「白衣仙长」四个字上烫了一下，又烫了一下，一直烫到他爬出那道石缝，还没有凉。

长廊里漆黑一片，三天里，火把早烧完了。走出几十步，前头黑里有脚步声，走几步，停一停，又走几步。小满蹲下去，搭上了箭壶里最后一支箭，拉满了。山里的规矩，谁先出声，谁先死。弦快松的时候，对面小声道：「……沈师兄？我听见弓弦响了，外门背弓的，只有你。……萝卜，还你。」

是孙二狗。小满把弓放下了，手心里全是汗。孙二狗灰袍从领口撕到了腰，额角肿着一个青包，十个指甲劈了好几个：「掉进翻板坑了。坑底那条旧水道干了，壁上有铜，我抠了半块。……还有两个人，不动了。我喊，人都在抢灵草。后来坑口伸下来一截剑鞘，一个穿淡蓝衣裳的师姐把我拽了上来，又掰了半块干粮塞给我。旁边有人叫她秦师姐。……我吃的是她那半块。」他双手递过那根萝卜来，完完整整，一口没咬。小满把他的手推了回去：「你留着。往后在黑里，别先出声。」孙二狗道：「那……我怎么知道是你？」小满答不上来。

又走出一段，前头黑里又有脚步声，一样地走几步，停一停。孙二狗张嘴要说话，小满一把捂住了他的嘴，没有等，一箭射了过去。黑里「啊」的一声，有人倒在地上，抱着腿往后爬，爬远了。小满摸过去，地上丢着一把刀，刀刃是黏的——血是别人的。孙二狗在他身后抖成一团。小满的手，这一回没有停。

长廊的尽头，离石门只剩几十步，横着一块青石板，一丈见方，叫称石。它只称出去的人：人踩上去，石面上便亮起几道纹，几道纹，便是几层。要出秘境，只这一条道，谁也绕不过去。石板四周围了一圈人，踩一个，哄一声：「二层！」「三层——不赖！」一个本观的老弟子踩上去，亮了四道，旁边一齐叫好。

小满挤在人堆后头，手心里全是汗。他如今是四层，一脚踩上去，要是亮出四道纹来，跟方才那个老弟子一般多，谁也不会看错。孙二狗先挤到前头去了。他想起地图上那个翻板坑，坑边一行小字：「坑底有旧水道，通长廊尽头。」他掉头往回走，走到那块第三石板跟前，一脚踩了上去。石板一翻，他掉进了坑里。坑底果然有一道旧水道，水道口横着两个人，没有动。他正要猫腰钻进去，头顶上一暗，一截剑鞘伸了下来，坑口蹲着一个穿淡蓝衣裳的师姐：「抓着。」他只得抓住，装着手脚发软，蹬两下，滑一下——可那剑鞘上，从头到尾没吃着他半分分量。上了坑口，那师姐低头看了看自己握鞘的手，道：「你没往下坠。」说完便走，一脚踩上称石，石面上亮了六道纹。

小满到底没有再下去。他把一身的灵气往里收，收了又收，一脚踩上称石——石面上亮了一道，又亮了一道，便不亮了。「二层！」有人笑，「五行杂灵根，进去三天，还是二层！」他低着头走了过去。那两道纹，是他把一口气死死憋在丹田底下，憋得耳朵里嗡嗡响，硬压出来的；再多站一口气的工夫，第三道便要亮了。

三天后，潮水要回来了。鲁泥鳅拿一根芦苇插在泥里，看了半天，道：「比上回早了半个时辰。」观主玄沉子还站在石门前，两只手拢在袖子里，像是这三天，他一步也没有挪过。他身边多了一张小木桌，周衡坐在桌后，账簿摊开，出来一个，收一块名牌，勾一个。玄沉子不看人脸，看的是名牌。头一拨出来的是内门那一行，进去二十几个，出来少了一个，袍子上没破几处，名牌是内门自己收的。剩下那四个九层，袖子都是鼓的；不出一个月，四个都闭了关冲筑基——腊月的大比只比练气，台上最高的，便剩了八层的祁长松。青袍们出来得也早，个个怀里鼓鼓的，有两个袖口上是黑的，是干了的血。冯九掌心托着一粒指甲盖大的珠子，一跳一跳：「息珠。十年一口气，就凝这么几粒。」冯九回头望了一眼那道石门，跟他师弟道：「卖名牌的门派，是穷了。下一回，咱们不买。」周衡的笔尖顿了一顿，又勾了下去。

起先是一个一个地出来，后来是三个五个，再后来，隔好一阵才出来一个。周衡的笔，勾着勾着，便停在了半空里。岸上那几个提食盒的家丁，伸着脖子等，等到人都稀了，有一个还在等，食盒的盖子揭开又盖上。冯九拿那只少了两根指头的手，把赤松观出来的人数了一遍，走到桌前：「赤松观进去十二个，出来五个。少的那几个，叫什么？」周衡翻了翻账，头也不抬：「名牌没还。秘境里，各凭本事。」

阿禾蹲在河滩上一块石头旁边，看见他，站起身来：「捡到什么了？」小满道：「一撮土。」阿禾道：「……土？」小满道：「土。你呢？」阿禾摊开手心，是一小块布，布里三粒黑东西：「谷。很老很老。有人在秘境里头种过地。」她脖子上一圈燎泡，拿领子遮着。她翻开本子，「地图钱，五十文，白花了」那一行底下，添了一行：**又：地图背给人听了一遍，换回一条命。不白花。**小满没说话，心里却一动：石室南墙上那个背着筐、往水里撒土的人，撒过的地方，长出了地。

阿禾走了两步，又回过头来，上上下下打量了他一回，道：「你是不是……长高了？」小满后背一紧，把自己往矮里缩了一寸，道：「秘境里冷，缩了三天，一出来，伸开了。」阿禾把他从头看到脚，道：「冷的人，缩着才对。」说完转身走了，没有掏本子。

石门快要合上的时候，马小宝他们才出来。四个跟班一个架着一个，饿得两眼发青，嘴唇上全是舔石头舔出来的血口子；马小宝一身簇新的法衣糊满了泥，脸肿得像一只发面馒头，走在最前头，谁多看一眼，他便瞪谁。出来的是五个。

周衡提着笔，勾到第五个，抬起头来，往石门里望了一眼：「孟有田呢？」

小满这才知道，老蔫叫孟有田。认得这个人快两个月，头一回听见他的名字。

马小宝的嘴唇动了两动，道：「他自己爬的。」一个跟班抢着道：「走错了，走到左边那道崖上，碰着了前人的阵，粘了三天。孟有田自己要往上爬，没扒住。」没有一个人提沈小满——提了沈小满，便得先说自己带着一盘麻绳爬下那道崖，是去做什么的；那张脸是谁打的，他也一个字不提。周衡看着马小宝，看了很久。马小宝把脸扭开了。

潮水漫上来了，漫过淤泥滩，漫过石门的门楣。周衡把账簿上那一页的数加了一遍：**名牌，进去四百一十七块，收回一百八十三块。**死在里头的，比活着出来的多。他把账簿翻到最后几页，那几页的纸比别的黄，提笔写下「孟有田」三个字，在底下画了一道红杠，画得很直，很慢；写完一个，又写一个。外卖名牌那一页底下，他添了一行：**收回五十二块。**小满站在人堆里，看着他写，写到天黑，还没有写完。

石门前那个拢着手的人，听到「左边那道崖」几个字的时候，眼皮动了一动。玄沉子在河滩上一百八十几个一身泥的人里，一个一个看过去。看到小满的时候，停了一停。他朝小满招了招手，温和地问：「往哪边走的？」小满道：「右边。人多。」玄沉子低头看了看他的草鞋。草鞋帮子上，沾着几点青苔，湿的，绿得发黑——左边那道石阶上长的青苔，右边的长廊是干的。玄沉子看了一会儿，笑了一笑，道：「右边人多。」说完这一句，便不再看他了。小满站回人群里，低着头，数自己草鞋上的泥点子，数到第十七个，后背上的汗才下去。
story.en:
Meanwhile — that day Xiaoman went left, and A He went right: more people on the right, so the knife comes down on somebody else first — but more knives come down on the right, too.

She went by the map in her head. At the door of the second chamber, the third flagstone tips when you tread on it — she stood beside it and shouted, "Don't step on the third one!" One heard; one didn't hear in time, was elbowed aside by a young gentleman in brocade behind and dropped through, and an "ow!" came up out of the pit in Sun Ergou's voice. The crowd pushed her on; she looked back and shouted again; no one answered.

The stone bridge was narrow, room for one. When she reached the near end, two men had run into each other in the dark in the middle of the bridge, one of the abbey's grey robes and a green robe of the Green Duckweed school; they stopped three paces apart, neither able to see the other's face. They stood a long time, neither moving, neither giving way. The grey robe reached into his coat — and the green robe's sword was out first. The grey robe went down; what he'd been gripping was a fire-starter. The green robe stepped over him and crossed. A He crouched behind a rock at the bridgehead for a stick of incense before she dared go over.

In the herb garden past the bridge, the last plant had been pulled up by the roots. Two old disciples of the abbey pressed a young gentleman in brocade into the mud and held him there till he stopped moving, then let go and crouched in the mud to share the plant, half each; then they turned out his purse — five spirit stones, two each, and for the odd one the two of them played finger-guessing. The dry riverbed below the garden was drawn on the map as water; this year the water had sunk low and bared its bottom, and every crack was thick with spirit herbs, high, middle and low grade alike, and a vein of copper ran along the wall. Everyone poured down into it. There was only one way down, a stone step one person wide. At its lip stood the inner court's Qi Changsong, layer eight, both feet nailed there; the crowd surged up to him, pushed him, shoved him, like water against a post — he didn't move, and it split around him and flowed back. Below the step the four layer nines were stripping the herbs clump by clump, each clump into a sleeve, not even looking at the grade. When they had enough and came up, Qi Changsong moved aside one step.

A He didn't join the scramble. She went round to the riverbed's edge; there lay a patch of ground, black, black and shiny, not a blade of grass on it — just like her family's hillside field in Shi'ao Village. At the edge of the black ground, of all places, a plant had come up, three leaves, purple shot with gold: "Purple-whisker zhi, one plant worth three spirit stones." Three spirit stones were a month's allowance in the outer court. She crouched; the black earth loosened under her fingers and showed half of something, black, hard as a pebble: grain, grain that looked burnt. She dug further down with her fingernail — under that black ground, row on row, laid out neat and even. Long, long ago, someone had farmed here. The purple-whisker zhi's roots were wound right through that row of grain: pull the plant, and roots and grain came up together in a mess of mud; dig the grain, and the plant was lost. She lowered her head and, one grain at a time, dug out three.

As she dug out the third, the back of her neck went hot. A fire snake a foot long lay across her shoulder, its head against her neck, so hot the fine hairs curled one by one. The man behind her was all smiles, fair-faced, ochre-robed: "Little girl, what are you crouched there looking for? Picking up dirt?" He bent, pulled up the purple-whisker zhi by the roots and tucked it into his coat. "This garden's picked bare. That map of yours — give it here." "There's no map," said A He. "I learned it by heart." "Then recite it. Get one word wrong —" The fire snake tightened, and the ring of flesh round her neck sizzled. So A He recited: how many steps before each turn in the corridor, which flagstone would tip, three chambers, the stone bridge, the garden, all in one breath, not one word wavering, and at the end: "Left cliff. Three went down ten years ago; one came up… nobody goes." "Oh," said the man. "Where nobody goes is where the things are." The fire snake slid off her neck and back into the gourd. He went back the way he'd come, fast.

A He crouched at the edge of the black ground and didn't get up for a long time. There was a ring of blisters round her neck; she grabbed a handful of cool earth and held it there. She wrapped the three black grains in a scrap of cloth and put them beside the thirty seed grains sewn into the front of her jacket, took out her notebook and wrote: **First of the eleventh month. Hidden realm. Purple-whisker zhi, one, let go. Grain: three, black, not edible.** Then, after a thought, one more line: **Someone farmed here.**

After daybreak on the third day there was no sound from the cliff. Xiaoman sat before the altar, his hands still shaking. He spread his notebook on his knee and turned to the back page — five lines Master Chu had chanted, swaying, before the bell, and then rapped the desk with his ruler: "From the Book of Documents. Learn them!" Xiaoman read them once under his breath: "Water soaks and descends; fire blazes and rises; wood bends and straightens; metal yields and takes new form; earth is sown and reaped." The voice in the token said lazily: "Five tempers. Earth is what things grow in — what grows nothing isn't earth. Push them round once."

So he pushed. A coolness rose from his dantian, turned hot at a bend, sank into warmth, hardened into his bones, cooled and seeped back down — wood, fire, earth, metal, water, once round. He thought of the stove at home: wood to fire, fire to ash, ash to feed the field, stalks from the field, stalks dried and back into the stove. What Master Chu had wagged his head over for half a lesson, his mother did every day of her life. His hands stopped shaking.

At noon that day Xiaoman closed the empty jade box and set it back square in the middle of the altar; then he crouched by the four empty pits and measured once more with his hand: seven spans, right. He scraped a pinch of the cauldron moss off a rim and wrapped it in his handkerchief. He cupped his fists to the four pits — he couldn't have said why — and Yinyue didn't ask whom he was saluting.

He went out through the wall. It stood open behind him, the iron pot still lying in its hollow, the sword in its neck. The blue-white ring on the cliff still glowed and five people still hung there, too hungry even to groan. At the very outer edge, right by the black mouth, a grey robe was still stuck to the rock, both sleeves spread, its collar torn open, empty, no one in it, held to the stone by the ring of light as if someone had just stepped out of it. By the rusted spike on the ledge's edge there were a few fresh white scratches on the rim — fingernail scratches, each shorter than the last.

Xiaoman stood a while by those white scratches. He did not look into the dark.

He didn't leave. He sat down by the iron spike, his back to the cliff, the notched knife across his knees, and waited. A hunter waits a whole day for one deer; that is nothing.

An hour before the stone door shut, the blue-white ring on the cliff went out. Five people dropped thump, thump onto the ledge, lay there a long while, and got up one by one. In the dark Ma Xiaobao made out the one sitting by the spike, and his eyes slowly lit: "…A layer two." His voice was hoarse with hunger, but the smile was the same smile. "Three days without food — still enough to deal with you." He lunged.

Xiaoman stood and met him with a fist to the bridge of the nose.

"One."

Ma Xiaobao rocked back, and before he had finished rocking the second fist came. "Two." Xiaoman counted them out one by one, not fast, not slow, the way his father skinned a rabbit, in order: nose, left ribs, right ribs, belly. Of his layer-four strength he used three parts in ten — use it all and the man would be gone. The four followers stood in a row against the foot of the cliff; not one dared move, and he touched none of them. At "twenty-three" the last blow, neither hard nor soft, landed on Ma Xiaobao's shoulder, like a seal stamped on the business.

Ma Xiaobao lay curled on the ground with his arms over his head, both eyes swollen to slits. Xiaoman crouched beside him: "Twelfth of the tenth month, the woodshed, twenty-three. Paid back. Not one more, not one less." He stood to go, and a voice came up from the ground, pitched very low: "Shen Xiaoman."

Xiaoman stopped. Face to the rock, Ma Xiaobao said, word by word: "Inside the wall — what did you hear?" "I heard," said Xiaoman. Ma Xiaobao was silent a good while before he spoke again: "Before we came in, my father's letter came. In the twelfth month he's coming by boat himself, bringing me pills, and a mirror — the one the immortal in white handed my father himself, in your yard, on the night of the fifth of the first month; I was the one holding the torch. The immortal said: catch something with it, and there's a reward." He panted. "On the contest stage, in front of the whole temple, I'll hold it up to you. Whatever you did behind that wall these three days — it'll show. And whatever you heard — up on that stage, you won't get one word of it out."

Xiaoman didn't answer. At the words "immortal in white" the token on his chest went hot, then hot again, and it was still hot when he had climbed out through the crack.

The long corridor was pitch black; in three days the torches had long burned out. A few dozen steps on there were footsteps in the dark ahead: a few steps, a pause, a few more. Xiaoman crouched, nocked the last arrow in his quiver, and drew it full. The rule of the hills: whoever makes the first sound dies first. Just as the string was about to slip, a small voice came from ahead: "…Brother Shen? I heard a bowstring. In the outer court you're the only one who carries a bow. …The radish — it's yours."

It was Sun Ergou. Xiaoman lowered the bow; his palms were all sweat. Sun Ergou's grey robe was torn from collar to waist, a blue lump swelled on his brow, and several of his ten fingernails were split: "Fell into the tipping-slab pit. The old drain down there has gone dry, and there's copper in the wall — I dug out half a lump. …There were two more people, not moving. I shouted, but everyone was fighting over herbs. Then a scabbard came down over the edge — a senior sister in pale blue hauled me up, and broke off half her ration and pushed it at me. Somebody near called her Sister Qin. …What I ate was her half." He held out the radish in both hands, whole, not one bite gone. Xiaoman pushed his hands back: "Keep it. From now on, in the dark, don't make the first sound." "Then… how will I know it's you?" Xiaoman had no answer.

Further on, there were footsteps in the dark ahead again, the same: a few steps, a pause. Sun Ergou opened his mouth to speak; Xiaoman clapped a hand over it and, without waiting, loosed an arrow. A cry in the dark — someone fell, clutching a leg, and crawled away backward till he was gone. Xiaoman felt his way over: a knife lay on the ground, its blade sticky — the blood was someone else's. Behind him Sun Ergou was shaking all over. Xiaoman's hand, this time, hadn't paused.

At the end of the long corridor, only a few dozen steps from the stone door, lay a bluestone slab ten feet square, called the Weighing Stone. It weighed only those going out: step on it and lines lit up on its face — so many lines, so many layers. To leave the realm there was only this way; no one could go round. A ring of people stood round the slab, and at each one who stepped on it a roar went up: "Layer two!" "Three — not bad!" One of the abbey's seniors stepped on and lit four, and a cheer went up.

Xiaoman was squeezed at the back of the crowd, his palms all sweat. He was at layer four now; if he stepped on and four lines lit, as many as that senior, nobody would mistake it. Sun Ergou had already pushed his way to the front. He remembered the tipping-slab pit on the map and the small note beside it: "Old drain at the bottom of the pit, leads to the end of the corridor." He turned and went back to the third flagstone and stepped on it. The slab tipped and he dropped into the pit. At the bottom, sure enough, was an old drain, two people lying across its mouth, not moving. He was about to stoop into it when the light above went dim and a scabbard came down; at the lip crouched a senior sister in pale blue: "Grab hold." He had to grab it, and made a show of weak arms and legs, kick twice, slip once — but from first to last the scabbard never took half an ounce of his weight. At the lip she looked down at the hand that held the scabbard and said: "You didn't hang." Then she walked off, stepped onto the Weighing Stone, and six lines lit on its face.

Xiaoman didn't go down again after all. He drew his qi in, and in again, and stepped onto the Weighing Stone — one line lit, then another, and no more. "Layer two!" someone laughed. "Five-element mixed roots, three days inside, still layer two!" He walked across with his head down. Those two lines he had forced down with a breath pinned hard below his dantian till his ears rang; a breath longer on the stone and the third would have lit.

Three days later the tide was coming back. Lu the Loach pushed a reed into the mud, studied it a good while and said: "Half an hour earlier than last time." Abbot Xuanchenzi still stood before the stone door with his hands in his sleeves, as if he hadn't moved a step in three days. Beside him now stood a little wooden table; Zhou Heng sat behind it with the ledger open: one out, one name tablet taken back, one tick. Xuanchenzi didn't look at faces; he looked at the tablets. The inner-court file came out first: twenty-odd had gone in, one fewer came out, their robes hardly torn, and the inner court took back its own tablets. The four layer nines left had bulging sleeves; within the month all four had gone into seclusion to break through to Foundation — and the twelfth-month contest was for Qi Refining only, so the highest left on the platform would be Qi Changsong, layer eight. The green robes came out early too, every one with a bulging coat; two had black cuffs — dried blood. In Feng Jiu's palm lay a bead the size of a fingernail, beating: "Breath pearl. Ten years of one breath, and only a few of these." Feng Jiu looked back once at the stone door and said to his junior: "A school that sells its tablets has gone poor. Next time, we don't buy." Zhou Heng's brush paused, then ticked on.

At first they came out one by one, then in threes and fives, and after that only one every long while. Zhou Heng's brush, ticking and ticking, stopped in midair. The servants with food boxes on the bank craned their necks and waited; when the people had thinned out, one was still waiting, lifting the lid of his box and putting it back. Feng Jiu, with the hand missing two fingers, counted the Red Pine people who'd come out, and went to the table: "The Red Pine Abbey went in twelve and came out five. The ones missing — what were their names?" Zhou Heng turned a page of the ledger without looking up: "Tablets not returned. In the hidden realm, each by his own skill."

A He was crouching by a rock on the flats; seeing him she stood. "Find anything?" "A pinch of earth." "…Earth?" "Earth. You?" She opened her hand: a scrap of cloth, three black things in it. "Grain. Very, very old. Someone farmed inside the hidden realm." There was a ring of blisters round her neck; she kept it hidden under her collar. She opened her notebook, and under the line "Map money, fifty cash, wasted" she added another: **Also: recited the map for someone once; got a life back for it. Not wasted.** Xiaoman said nothing, but something stirred in him: the man on the chamber's south wall with the basket on his back, scattering earth into the water — where he scattered, land grew.

A He took two steps, turned back and looked him up and down. "Have you… grown?" Xiaoman's back went tight; he shrank himself an inch: "It was cold in there. I was hunched up three days, and when I came out I stretched." A He looked him over from head to foot. "People who are cold ought to stay hunched." She turned and went, and didn't take out her notebook.

Only as the stone door was about to shut did Ma Xiaobao's lot come out. Four followers held each other up, eyes blue with hunger, lips split from licking stone; Ma Xiaobao, his brand-new robe caked in mud, his face swollen like a steamed bun, walked in front and glared at anyone who looked. Five came out.

Zhou Heng, brush in hand, had ticked his way to the fifth when he looked up and peered into the stone door. "Meng Youtian?"

Only then did Xiaoman learn that Old Wilt's name was Meng Youtian. He had known the man nearly two months and was hearing his name for the first time.

Ma Xiaobao's lips moved twice. "He climbed by himself." A follower got in quickly: "Took a wrong turn, ended up on the left cliff, hit some old binding, stuck three days. Meng Youtian tried to climb up on his own and lost his grip." Not one of them mentioned Shen Xiaoman — mention him, and first they'd have to say what they had climbed down that cliff for with a coil of hemp rope; and who had done that face, he didn't say a word about either. Zhou Heng looked at Ma Xiaobao a long time. Ma Xiaobao turned his face away.

The tide came in, over the mudflats, over the lintel of the stone door. Zhou Heng added up the figures on that page of the ledger: **Name tablets: 417 went in; 183 returned.** More had died inside than came out alive. He turned the ledger to its last few pages, the ones yellower than the rest, took up his brush and wrote the three characters Meng Youtian, and drew a red stroke beneath them — very straight, very slow; when one was done, he wrote another. At the bottom of the page for tablets sold to outsiders, he added one line: **Returned: 52.** Xiaoman stood in the crowd and watched him write; by nightfall he still hadn't finished.

The man standing before the stone door with his hands in his sleeves — at the words "the left cliff" his eyelids flickered. Xuanchenzi looked over the hundred and eighty-odd mud-caked people on the flats one by one. At Xiaoman he paused. He beckoned to him and asked mildly: "Which way did you go?" "Right. More people." The abbot looked down at his straw sandals. On their sides clung a few flecks of moss, wet, green going on black — the moss of the steps on the left; the corridor on the right was dry. Xuanchenzi looked a while, smiled, and said: "More people on the right." And with that he didn't look at him again. Xiaoman went back into the crowd. Head down, he counted the mud spots on his sandals; at the seventeenth, the sweat on his back finally dried.

label.en: Enough for today — the contest is tomorrow

exits.means: rests for the day, waits for tomorrow's contest

story.zh:
小满去执事房领小狰。小狰趴在账簿上，睡得四脚朝天，肚子鼓得像一只小西瓜。周衡翻开巡夜簿，在十月那一页底下添了一行小字：**上旬丢十株。收狰至今，一株未失。另议。**小满问：「另议什么？」周衡道：「腊八结账。」

小满抱起小狰，走到门口，又站住了，回过头来：「周师兄。孟……孟师兄家里，谁去说？」周衡没有抬头，算盘珠子也停了。隔了一会儿，他道：「我。」

第二天一早，伙房的大锅少熬了一半粥，饭堂里空出一大片位子。头一天，还有人往那片空位子上看；第三天，便没人看了。周衡把名册上剩下的一百三十一个名字重新誊过，预备腊月初一的灵石。窗户底下那张铺空着，铺上叠着一床薄被，被头上压着一团叠得方方正正的油纸，一直没人去动。

那天夜里，小满把小狰揣进怀里，往柴房去。路过正殿后头，他站住了：殿里点着一盏灯笼。观主玄沉子跪在那口空石座跟前，张着一只手，拇指抵着石面正中那块颜色深些的四方印子，一拃一拃地量过去。量完了，他跪在那里，半天没动，轻轻道了一句：「……不在那里了。」等灯笼挪开了，小满进殿蹲到石座跟前，张开手掌，一拃，两拃……七拃。另一边，也是七拃。跟石室里那四个空坑，一般大。祖师给它留了一口石座，留了三百年，它一天也没有在这石座上站过。

到了柴房后头，月亮很亮。他盘腿坐下，掏出那个红糖包纸订的小本子，翻到恩仇簿那几页，提起笔，写下：**冬月初一。左崖。邹青松。**这一笔，他记在自己名下。又写：**冬月初二夜。左崖。孟有田。**笔尖悬在那里，悬了很久。这一笔，记在马小宝名下，还是记在他自己名下，他不知道。他又往前翻，翻到「十月十二。柴房。廿三下。马小宝。」那一行，在杠底下空着的那一格里，一笔一画地写：**冬月初三。左崖。还讫。**

他把本子翻到最后一页，那一页上什么也没有。他想了很久。长廊里那个胖公子，荷包里有一道保命的符；他的三支箭，没有一支伤着那个人；他活下来，靠的是一匹画歪了的马，一只他杀了的龟，和一个拼掉了一截尾巴的妖王。下一回，这三样，一样也未必在。他写：**沈小满，欠沈小满：下回，自己打得过，护得住人。**写完了，在底下画了一道杠，杠底下空着一格，留着写还的那一天。

他从怀里摸出那一块灵石——冬月初一剩下的那一块——握在手心，吸了一口。只一口，那块灵石便一凉，暗下去一层，像蒙了灰。他赶紧撒了手。从前是漏勺，一块灵石，他要吸上小半个月；如今是水缸，再吸一口，它就是一把粉了。他把它揣回怀里，在心里算：一个月三块，交公中两块，剩一块，一口；离腊月初八，还有三十五天。

他小声道：「银月。」木牌没有回答。他等了很久，木牌里那个声音开口了：「石室里那个故事，你还要不要听？」他说要。她便讲，讲得又快又硬，像是怕一停下来就讲不下去：「当年发大水，淹了九州。有个人叫鲧，从天帝那里把那土偷了出来，往洪水里撒——水涨一尺，土长一丈。天帝叫火神把他杀在羽山。他儿子叫禹，禹不堵，他疏，把那土一把一把铺平了，定下九州，铸了九口鼎，一州一口。《山海经》{典=shanhai-xirang}上，这件事只有几行字。」她顿了一顿，「……本王记得的，比书上多。」小满道：「那九口鼎，后来呢？」又隔了很久，一个很轻很轻的声音：「……后来，沉了。」柴房外头，远远的，泗水涨满了，一下一下地拍着岸，很慢，很匀，像是有人在河底下，慢慢地呼吸。

那以后的夜里，他练功不为账，也不为藏。他在柴房后头拉那张弓，拉满，松开，再拉满——《落雁三箭》，他只会头一箭，爷爷一辈子没射下过大雁；他射下来的，是一只葫芦塞子——拉完了，拿那把缺了三个牙的短刀，对着一根木桩，一刀一刀地练他爹放鹿血的那一下。练完了，坐下来吐纳，一口一口，把水缸往满里灌，灌到半满，自己停下来。

有一天挑水路过山门，瞿老在第三百级上扫地。小满站住了，看那把扫帚，看了很久。瞿老头也不抬，只把扫帚往旁边让了一让：「腿稳。」

腊月初七，离冬月初一周衡在执事房门口说的那个日子，只剩一天了。明日腊八，宗门大比，内门外门一起比，五行台。冠军，筑基丹一枚——全观一年，就这一颗。
story.en:
Xiaoman went to the stewards' office to fetch the little zheng. It lay on the ledger asleep with all four paws in the air, belly round as a small melon. Zhou Heng opened the night-watch book and added a small line under the tenth month: **Ten lost in the first ten days. Since the zheng was taken, not one lost. To be settled.** "Settled how?" asked Xiaoman. "Accounts close on Laba," said Zhou Heng.

Xiaoman picked up the little zheng and got as far as the door, then stopped and turned back. "Brother Zhou. Meng… Brother Meng's family — who'll tell them?" Zhou Heng didn't raise his head; the abacus beads stopped too. After a while he said: "Me."

Early next morning the kitchen cooked half as much porridge in the big pot, and a great stretch of seats in the refectory stood empty. The first day, people still glanced at the empty seats; by the third, no one looked. Zhou Heng copied out fresh the hundred and thirty-one names left on the roll and set aside the spirit stones for the first of the twelfth month. The bunk under the window stood empty; on it lay a thin quilt, folded, and on the quilt a wad of oiled paper folded square and neat, which nobody touched.

That night Xiaoman tucked the little zheng into his coat and headed for the woodshed. Passing behind the main hall, he stopped: a lantern was lit inside. Abbot Xuanchenzi was kneeling before the empty stone plinth, one hand spread, his thumb on the darker square mark in the middle of the stone, spanning across it hand over hand. When he'd done he knelt there a long while without moving, and said softly: "…It isn't there any more." When the lantern had gone, Xiaoman went in, crouched at the plinth, spread his hand: one span, two… seven. The other side, seven too. The same size as the four empty pits in the chamber. The founder had kept a stone plinth for it, kept it three hundred years, and not for one day had it ever stood there.

Behind the woodshed the moon was bright. He sat cross-legged, took out the little notebook sewn from red-sugar wrapping paper, turned to the pages of his ledger of debts and favours, took up the brush and wrote: **First of the eleventh month. Left cliff. Zou Qingsong.** This one he entered under his own name. Then: **Second night of the eleventh month. Left cliff. Meng Youtian.** The brush hung there a long time. Whether this went under Ma Xiaobao's name or under his own, he didn't know. He turned further back, to the line **Twelfth of the tenth month. Woodshed. Twenty-three. Ma Xiaobao.**, and in the empty space under its stroke wrote, stroke by stroke: **Third of the eleventh month. Left cliff. Paid in full.**

He turned to the last page of the notebook; there was nothing on it. He thought a long time. The plump gentleman in the corridor had had a life-saving charm in his purse; of his three arrows, not one had so much as touched the man; he had lived through it on one badly drawn horse, a turtle he had killed, and a demon queen who had spent a length of her tail. Next time, not one of the three might be there. He wrote: **Shen Xiaoman, owed to Shen Xiaoman: next time, strong enough on my own to win, and to protect people.** When he'd done, he drew a line beneath it, and left a space under the line, for the day it was paid.

He took from his coat that one spirit stone — the one left over from the first of the eleventh month — held it in his palm and drew one breath. Just one, and the stone went cool and dimmed a shade, as if dust had settled on it. He let go at once. As a skimmer, one stone lasted him half a month; as a water vat, one more breath and it would be powder. He put it back in his coat and reckoned: three stones a month, two to the common fund, one left, one breath; thirty-five days to the eighth of the twelfth month.

"Yinyue," he whispered. The token didn't answer. He waited a long time, and then the voice in the token spoke: "That story in the stone chamber — do you still want to hear it?" He said he did. So she told it, fast and hard, as if afraid that stopping would stop it for good: "Long ago a great flood drowned the Nine Provinces. A man called Gun stole that earth from the Lord of Heaven and threw it into the flood — the water rose a foot, the earth grew ten. The Lord of Heaven had the fire god kill him on Mount Yu. His son was called Yu. Yu didn't dam; he drained; he spread that earth handful by handful, levelled it, fixed the Nine Provinces, and cast nine cauldrons, one for each province. In the Classic of Mountains and Seas this takes only a few lines." She paused. "…I remember more than the book." "And the nine cauldrons — then what?" After another long while, a very, very faint voice: "…Then they sank." Outside the woodshed, far off, the Si was at full tide, lapping the bank stroke after stroke, very slow, very even, as if someone at the bottom of the river were slowly breathing.

From then on he trained at night not for the accounts, nor for hiding. Behind the woodshed he drew the bow, full, released, full again — of Felling-Geese Three Arrows he knew only the first; his grandfather never in his life brought down a wild goose; what he had brought down was a gourd's plug — then he took the short knife with three notches in its blade and, at a wooden stake, practised over and over the one stroke his father used to bleed a deer. When that was done he sat and breathed, breath by breath, filling the vat toward full, and at half full stopped of his own accord.

One day, carrying water past the gate, he found Elder Qu sweeping on the three hundredth step. Xiaoman stopped and looked at the broom, looked a long time. Elder Qu didn't look up, only moved his broom aside: "Steady legs."

The seventh of the twelfth month: one day left before the date Zhou Heng named at the stewards' office door on the first of the eleventh. Tomorrow, Laba, the sect contest, inner court and outer court together, on the Five Elements Platform. Champion, one Foundation pill — one a year, for the whole temple.
